questions.q: What are the two basic types of curiosity described in lesson 1?
a: Diversive and epistemic
Passive and aggressive
Emotional and logical
Natural and learned
questions.why: Lesson 1 splits curiosity into diversive, which seeks novelty, and epistemic, which seeks deep understanding.

a: A craving for novelty that can be superficial and impulsive
A patient effort to master one difficult subject
A refusal to learn anything outside your profession
A habit of questioning every belief you hold
questions.why: Lesson 1 links diversive curiosity to clickbait and endless scrolling rather than deep study.

questions.q: What did Darwin's eight-year study of a barnacle illustrate?
a: The deep, sustained effort of epistemic curiosity
The shallow pull of diversive curiosity
The way curiosity fades with age
The value of avoiding difficult questions
questions.why: Lesson 1 uses the barnacle as the example of focused, long-term epistemic curiosity.

questions.q: How does the internet widen the gap between people, according to lesson 2?
a: The curious learn online while the incurious drift toward entertainment
Wealthy families can afford faster internet connections
Younger users understand technology better than older users
Schools teach different subjects depending on their funding
questions.why: Lesson 2 describes cognitive polarization between those who use the internet to learn and those who do not.

questions.q: What habit does the summary say wise people share?
a: They ask a lot of questions
They avoid unfamiliar topics
They trust their first instincts
They read only expert opinions
questions.why: Lesson 3 says the wisest people stay curious by continually asking questions.
